rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says using a verbal noun as an adjective adds emphasis or exaggeration.
rows.anchor: When a verbal noun is used as an adjective an element of exaggeration is incorporated in it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He explains Abraham’s declaration as total absolution from his people, severing every remaining relationship.
rows.anchor: I am totally absolved of you and there is no relationship left between you and me

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says Quraysh invoked their ancestors for polytheism while ignoring Abraham, their true ancestor, who rejected it, left his father and people, and settled his descendants in a barren valley; Abraham had brought them worldly and religious favors.
rows.anchor: greatest of their ancestors is Abraham (sws) because of whose blessings they were able to reap favours both in the corporal world and in their religion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The declaration addresses Abraham’s father first to warn Quraysh that their true inheritance is Abraham’s rejection of ancestral polytheism, not blind imitation of it.
rows.anchor: there is a warning to the Quraysh: if they contemplate they will realize that the real inheritance left by Abraham (sws) for them is not polytheism

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi reads Abraham’s people like Arabian idolaters: they acknowledged God but associated partners with Him; the exception therefore rejects their other deities as baseless.
rows.anchor: the nation of Abraham (sws) too did not disbelieve in God; it imputed partners to Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham worships and will continue to worship God because God created him and is therefore alone worthy of worship.
rows.anchor: he worships God and will do so in future because God is His creator and is thereby worthy of worship

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase relates to Abraham’s acquittal declaration, which he undertakes despite its hardship, trusting that God will guide him through it.
rows.anchor: the declaration of acquittal he is making is a very difficult one; he is aware of its hardships but he is hopeful

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative pronoun refers back to Abraham’s earlier declaration of acquittal and migration; similar pronouns occur in earlier sūrahs.
rows.anchor: is the declaration of acquittal and migration which is mentioned earlier. The occurrence of such pronouns can be seen in the previous sūrahs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bāqiyatan means an abiding tradition: Abraham implanted his acquittal declaration among his descendants through words, deeds, and teaching, for each generation to preserve and pass on.
rows.anchor: Abraham (sws) through his words, deeds and teachings implanted his declaration of acquittal as a firm tradition among his progeny

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi contrasts the branches of Abraham’s descendants: Israelites preserved the tradition through scripture and prophets, while it weakened among Ishmaelites, though a group retained monotheism and abhorrence of polytheism.
rows.anchor: In one of the branches of Abraham’s progeny, the Israelites, it was kept alive through their scriptures and through the teachings and reminders of their prophets

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tradition serves descendants as a signpost for returning whenever Satan tempts them or they stray from the right path.
rows.anchor: this tradition was left among his progeny so that it continue to be a sign-post to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-haqq refers to the Qur’an; Islahi supplies omitted wording about time passing and hearts hardening, citing the matching context at 57:16 and a related account at 21:44.
rows.anchor: in S ūrah al-Ḥadīd verse sixteen these words can be found in exactly the same context. Moreover, in verse 44 of Sūrah al-Anbiyā’ also this topic

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi calls Quraysh’s stated objection—that the Qur’an opposes their ancestors’ religion—a lame and frivolous pretext.
rows.anchor: lame and frivolous talk on their part that they are opposing the Qur’ ān because it calls them to what is against the religion of their ancestors

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi identifies the actual motive as prolonged worldly prosperity hardening their hearts; they fear accepting the Qur’an would threaten their worldly interests.
rows.anchor: their forefathers with the favours of this world and a great amount of time has passed over this opulence which has hardened their hearts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s truth and inimitable style naturally move people who are neither selfish nor afraid that its reality threatens their leadership.
rows.anchor: Since the Qur’ ān is nothing but the truth as is evident from the word and its style is also inimitable

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh called the Qur’an sorcery to recast its eloquence as human verbal magic like poetry and oratory; calling it worthless would have made their own audience think them foolish.
rows.anchor: they would try to convince their masses that the eloquence and articulacy found in the Qur’ ān is not because it is divine

rows.speaker: Quraysh leaders
rows.claim: Quraysh leaders argued that if God revealed the Qur’an, it should have been sent to a great chief of Makkah or Ṭā’if.
rows.anchor: if this book has been revealed by God, then why is not sent down to some great chief of Makkah or Ṭā’if

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The “two cities” are Makkah and Ṭā’if, centers of Arab nobles and chiefs and longstanding seats of leadership; the objection sought to persuade people that guidance should go to their affluent elites rather than the poor Prophet.
rows.anchor: refer to Makkah and Ṭā’if because it was these two cities who were the centre of the nobles and chiefs of the Arabs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi reads the verse as answering Quraysh’s arrogance: their wealth comes from God’s distribution, and differing fortunes show that they do not control it; God gives more or less by His wisdom.
rows.anchor: The fact is that the resources and riches the Quraysh have been blessed with are because of the distribution from God; they have not obtained them by themselves

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression means that one person puts another into his service.
rows.anchor: would mean that such and such a person put such and such a person into his service

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Different social and material levels enable mutual cooperation and service, which is the wisdom behind their distribution.
rows.anchor: these words express the wisdom behind granting different levels to different people viz a viz their mental and material resources and abilities: in order that people spend a life of mutual co-operation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the world is a trial, everyone depends on others: neither the greatest king nor the humblest person is self-sufficient, and everyone has some social utility.
rows.anchor: The Almighty has made this world for trial and test. For this reason, He has created its system in such a manner that every person is dependent on another in some way

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unequal abilities and resources create complementary social roles; every role is essential and none is less important, so society must care for even its smallest parts according to their benefit.
rows.anchor: All these elements are essential in fact indispensable for the development of a society. All provide different types of services; none of them is less in importance than the other
